episode.narrationText:
Almond Butter (Unsweetened)!

-

Ranked!

-

55.5 grams of fat. Saturated fat, omega3, and polyunsaturated fat are doing most of the work. For nuts, fat quality has to justify the calorie density.

-

18.8 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For a nut, this is mostly about fat quality and support.

-

21.2 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein is support here, not the whole argument.

-

Vitamin e at 40% daily value stands out most. That gives this food real vitamin support.

-

Magnesium at 61% daily value, zinc at 21% daily value, iron at 20% daily value stand out most. That gives this food real mineral support.

-

On the plus side: still a recognisable whole-food option. That keeps them cleaner than most processed snacks. Holds up as a better snack default than most packaged options. That real-world swap value counts. Fat and texture help satiety. They can hold up better than many snack foods.

-

The drawbacks next: spread form makes overdoing it easier. Still good, but less self-limiting than whole nuts. Portion control can get slippery fast. Dense foods punish casual handful math. Calorie density is very high. That makes portion control a real issue.

-

Almond Butter (Unsweetened) does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best in small amounts where the fats and minerals matter more than sheer calories.

-

B tier.

Baked Beans!

-

Ranked!

0.5 grams of fat. Saturated fat, omega3, and polyunsaturated fat are doing most of the work. For a legume, this is exactly the kind of profile you want.

-

27 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is where this starts to get messy. For legumes, the carbs look much better when fibre and protein are both backing them up.

-

5.5 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score is where things start to fall off. Protein support is a big part of what makes legumes worth it.

-

The rest is not doing much.

-

Minerals are basically not part of the case here.

-

On the plus side: cheap and convenient. Very easy to use as a quick meal component. Still keeps some fibre. Not completely nutritionally empty despite the weaker category fit. Has practical comfort-food appeal. People actually eat it, which matters in the real world.

-

The drawbacks next: added sugar is a major category problem. Legumes are supposed to win on slow-carb behaviour, and this pushes the opposite way. Processing drags the category fit down. The canned sweet-sauce format makes it a worse version of what legumes are supposed to be. Weak protein usefulness for a legume. It does not deliver the strong fibre-plus-protein combo that defines elite legumes.

-

Baked Beans does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only when convenience outweighs the weaker fibre or protein payoff.

-

D tier.

episode.narrationText:
Beetroot!

-

Ranked!

-

0.2 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For a tuber, the cleanest win is a more stable carb profile.

-

9.6 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is where this starts to get messy. For tubers, the carb side decides whether the food feels stable or flimsy.

-

1.6 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is usually limited here, so the other sections have to carry more.

-

Everything else is lackluster.

-

Minerals are basically not part of the case here.

-

The upsides first: practical staple carb source. Tubers are often judged by how usable they are day to day. Can be quite filling. A useful practical strength when the preparation stays sensible. Whole-food carb package. That matters because it is a cleaner baseline than heavily refined carbs.

-

Now the downsides: still a carb-heavy category. That is the core ceiling tubers have to manage. Satiety payoff depends a lot on format. Some versions are much steadier than others. Can go downhill fast when heavily processed. The category has a big preparation trap.

-

Beetroot does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only when you want easy carbs and can accept the missing upside.

-

D tier.

Black Beans!

Ranked!

-

The rest is pretty lackluster.

-

-

Black Beans has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want fibre, protein, and actual meal utility together.

-

-

-

B tier.

episode.narrationText:
Brown Rice!

-

Ranked!

-

2.9 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. Fat is basically not the story here.

-

77.2 grams of carbs. Glycemic index is where this starts to get messy. For grains, the carb quality matters much more than the raw number.

-

7.9 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein helps, but not enough if the carb side is weak.

-

Everything else is fairly underwhelming.

-

Magnesium at 35% daily value, zinc at 13% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still not a major mineral edge.

-

The upsides first: easy staple to build meals around. Very practical in everyday meal planning. Better category fit than white rice. At least retains more fibre and micronutrients than more refined versions. Often easy for people to tolerate. A practical plus in some contexts.

-

On the weaker side: fibre is only moderate for a strong grain. Not terrible, just not category-leading. Glycemic behaviour is only okay. Not one of the best grains on this dimension. Micronutrient payoff is fairly average. Does not stand out strongly in vitamins/minerals.

-

Brown Rice does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best when you want a staple carb that actually brings something useful with it.

-

B tier.

Brussels Sprouts!

-

Ranked!

-

0.3 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For a vegetable, nutrient payoff is the whole point.

-

3.4 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is not the main pitch here, but extra support still matters.

-

Vitamin k at 148% daily value, vitamin c at 94% daily value, vitamin a at 15% daily value stand out most. That is major vitamin support.

-

-

Pros first: makes meals feel more balanced. The category has real value beyond single-nutrient stats. Good volume for the calories. That matters for satiety and general usefulness. Very low downside whole food. Vegetables win a lot simply by offering clean nutritional payoff.

-

The drawbacks next: taste and texture can limit compliance. A strong paper profile still needs real-world repeatability. Energy density is very low. Good for some use cases, but not enough on its own. Usually needs pairing to make a full meal. Most vegetables are not complete by themselves.

-

Brussels Sprouts has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want low downside and easy micronutrient support.

-

S tier.

episode.narrationText:
Caraway Seeds!

-

Ranked!

-

14.6 grams of fat. Saturated fat, polyunsaturated fat, and omega3 are doing most of the work. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.

-

49.9 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For a seed, you want real nutrient concentration, not just tiny-food hype.

-

19.8 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.

-

Vitamin e at 17% daily value stands out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Magnesium at 68% daily value, iron at 91% daily value, calcium at 69% daily value stand out most. That is major mineral support.

-

Pros first: easy to sprinkle into meals. That practical versatility matters. Tiny food with serious nutrient density. Seeds often overperform for their size. Easy to sprinkle into meals for a real upgrade. Seeds often shine as support foods.

-

Now the downsides: real serving sizes are tiny. Like other spice-adjacent seeds, practicality trims the headline numbers. Paper scores can overstate realistic serving sizes. People often eat far less than 100 grams. Real serving sizes are often small. Some strong paper numbers are hard to cash out in practice.

-

Caraway Seeds does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best as a support food that boosts meals instead of carrying them alone.

-

B tier.

Carrots!

-

-

-

Great at some things, less absurdly dense overall than the very top vegetables. Protein is basically irrelevant. Not a real flaw, but still nearly absent.

-

episode.narrationText:
Chestnuts!

-

Ranked!

-

2.2 grams of fat. Saturated fat, polyunsaturated fat, and omega3 are doing most of the work. For nuts, fat quality has to justify the calorie density.

-

45.5 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For a nut, fat quality matters a ton.

-

2.4 grams of protein. Essential amino acids score is where things start to fall off. Protein is support here, not the whole argument.

-

Outside of that, the profile is pretty quiet.

-

Minerals are basically not part of the case here.

-

On the plus side: has strong seasonal appeal. Could be useful for content packaging even if the nutrition fit is weaker. Lighter than most nuts. This can be practically appealing to some viewers. Works in both sweet and savoury uses. Useful culinary flexibility.

-

Now the downsides: poor fit for the nut category goals. Very weak on the fat-quality signals that define stronger nuts. More starch-heavy than ideal here. Moves away from what the nut category is supposed to reward. Protein support is weak. Does not offer much in the protein-quality lane either.

-

Chestnuts does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only in small amounts when the calories stay under control.

-

D tier.

episode.narrationText:
Chia Seeds!

-

Ranked!

-

30.7 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.

-

42.1 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For a seed, the best ones punch way above their size.

-

16.5 grams of protein. Essential amino acid support is one of the better parts here. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.

-

Everything else is kind of whatever.

-

Magnesium at 80% daily value, zinc at 42% daily value, iron at 43% daily value stand out most. That gives this food real mineral support.

-

The upsides first: extreme fibre density. Adds standout digestive and satiety value even beyond the headline nutrient display. Can be very filling for the amount used. The gel-forming fibre profile gives it practical fullness value. Easy to add into meals. Can be mixed into oats, yogurt, puddings, and smoothies without much friction.

-

On the weaker side: contains some anti-nutrients. Phytates may reduce mineral uptake somewhat. Texture can put some people off. The gel-like texture is not universally appealing. Usually works best with some preparation. Often needs soaking or mixing into something else to shine.

-

Chia Seeds has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best as a support food that boosts meals instead of carrying them alone.

-

S tier.

Chickpeas!

-

Ranked!

-

6 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For a legume, this is exactly the kind of profile you want.

-

60.7 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For legumes, the carbs look much better when fibre and protein are both backing them up.

-

19.3 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein support is a big part of what makes legumes worth it.

-

Everything else here is pretty flat.

-

Iron at 34% daily value, magnesium at 29% daily value, zinc at 27% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still not a major mineral edge.

-

On the plus side: strong all-round legume profile. Fibre, minerals, and useful protein all show up well enough to make it a very solid category food. Easy to use across lots of meals. -

-

Chickpeas has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want fibre, protein, and actual meal utility together.

-

S tier.

Cornmeal!

-

Ranked!

-

3.9 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. Fat is basically not the story here.

-

79 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For grains, the carb quality matters much more than the raw number.

-

-

The rest is pretty lackluster.

-

Iron at 13% daily value, magnesium at 18% daily value, zinc at 12% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

The upsides first: can keep meals cheap and steady. That is a genuine category strength. Works as a meal anchor. A lot of value comes from being easy to build around. Usually affordable and scalable. Practicality matters for staple foods.

-

Now the downsides: needs strong pairings to feel complete. The grain rarely finishes the nutrition job alone. Protein quality is limited. Even the better grains usually need pairing. Carb load is still the main burden. That is the category risk no grain fully escapes.

-

Cornmeal does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best when you want a staple carb that actually brings something useful with it.

-

B tier.

Whole-Wheat Couscous!

-

Ranked!

0.6 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. Fat is basically not the story here.

-

-

12.8 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein helps, but not enough if the carb side is weak.

-

Everything else is fairly underwhelming.

-

Magnesium at 11% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

Pros first: usually affordable and scalable. Practicality matters for staple foods. Useful staple energy source. That matters because grains are often judged by how practical they are in real diets. Works as a meal anchor. A lot of value comes from being easy to build around.

-

Now the downsides: easy to overshoot portions. Staple carbs can pile up fast without much friction. Needs strong pairings to feel complete. The grain rarely finishes the nutrition job alone. Carb load is still the main burden. That is the category risk no grain fully escapes.

-

Whole-Wheat Couscous does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best when you want a staple carb that actually brings something useful with it.

-

Cream Cheese!

-

Ranked!

-

34 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For dairy, the fat side can either add richness or drag the whole thing down.

-

-

6.2 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Useful protein can rescue a lot of weaker traits here.

-

Vitamin b12 at 10% daily value, vitamin a at 22% daily value stand out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Calcium at 10% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

The upsides first: easy protein delivery for normal diets. Dairy gets real credit for convenience. Can be a very convenient protein vehicle. Convenience is one of dairy’s strongest practical advantages. Clear calcium identity. That is a core category strength.

-

On the weaker side: fat quality varies wildly across dairy. Some dairy is clean, some really is not. Some versions get dense fast on fat, sodium, or both. The category swings a lot by format. Processing changes the category a lot. The label alone does not tell the whole story.

-

Cream Cheese does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only when the taste or format matters more than getting the strongest dairy profile.

-

C tier.

Not everyone uses seeds consistently. Paper scores can overstate realistic serving sizes. People often eat far less than 100 grams.

-

Cumin Seeds does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best as a support food that boosts meals instead of carrying them alone.

-

B tier.

episode.narrationText:
Dates!

-

Ranked!

-

0.4 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For a fruit, being sweet is normal, but controlling it is what matters.

-

75 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For fruit, the real question is whether the sweetness stays under control.

-

2.5 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. For a fruit, you want sweetness to be kept in check.

-

The rest is pretty lackluster.

-

Potassium at 15% daily value, magnesium at 11% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

The upsides first: still brings some useful minerals. Not nutritionally empty despite the weak fruit fit. Can be useful in high-energy contexts. There are niche cases where the dense sugar load is useful. Still a recognisable whole fruit. That matters for fairness even when the category fit is weak.

-

On the weaker side: sugar density is a major category problem. Fruit is supposed to moderate sugar with fibre and payoff, and dates push the sugar side extremely hard. Glycemic behaviour is rough for fruit. Much weaker fit than fruits with gentler carb behaviour. Dried-fruit concentration makes the sugar hit even harsher. This is the cleanest reason dates should remain below ordinary whole fruits like grapes.

-

Dates does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only when the convenience or taste matters more than the nutrition return.

-

C tier.

episode.narrationText:
Greek Yogurt!

-

Ranked!

-

5 grams of fat. Cholesterol, saturated fat, and omega3 are doing most of the work. For dairy, the fat side can either add richness or drag the whole thing down.

-

3.9 grams of carbs. Sugar and glycemic index matter most here. For dairy, that is exactly the kind of thing you want.

-

9 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Useful protein can rescue a lot of weaker traits here.

-

Vitamin b12 at 22% daily value stands out most. That is only mild support overall.

-

Calcium at 11% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

On the plus side: fermented-food angle adds extra value. That gives it a practical benefit beyond the visible protein and fat numbers alone. Quite filling for the calories. The protein density gives it strong practical satiety value. Easy high-protein staple. Very easy to build meals or snacks around.

-

Now the downsides: saturated fat is not trivial. Still much cleaner than weak dairy foods, but not ultra-low-fat. Not suitable for everyone. Lactose tolerance and dairy tolerance vary. Healthiness can shift with toppings. Sugary add-ins can change the practical outcome fast.

-

Greek Yogurt has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when the protein payoff or fermentation angle outweighs the fat and sodium tradeoffs.

-

S tier.

Hemp Seeds!

-

Ranked!

48.8 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.

-

31.6 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.

-

Everything else here is pretty flat.

-

Magnesium at 175% daily value, zinc at 66% daily value, iron at 44% daily value stand out most. That is major mineral support.

-

-

-

-

Kiwi!

-

-

Vitamin c at 78% daily value stands out most. That is major vitamin support.

-

-

-

On the weaker side: can be easy to waste if timing is off. Perishability is a practical downside people actually feel. Protein contribution is tiny. That is normal for fruit, but it still limits nutritional breadth. Satiety is not especially strong. Fruit often needs help from the rest of the meal.

-

Kiwi has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want sweetness that still earns its place nutritionally.

-

episode.narrationText:
Macadamia Nuts!

-

Ranked!

-

75.8 grams of fat. Saturated fat is a major pressure point. For nuts, fat quality has to justify the calorie density.

-

13.8 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For a nut, you need enough upside to make the density worth it.

-

7.9 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is support here, not the whole argument.

-

Everything else is kind of whatever.

-

Magnesium at 31% daily value, zinc at 13% daily value, iron at 20% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still not a major mineral edge.

-

On the plus side: holds up as a better snack default than most packaged options. That real-world swap value counts. Texture helps them feel satisfying. That can make moderation easier than with softer snack foods. Still a recognisable whole-food option. That keeps them cleaner than most processed snacks.

-

The drawbacks next: protein is useful but not elite. Nuts help, but they are not protein stars. Calorie density is very high. That makes portion control a real issue. Cost or allergy issues can limit use. Practical downsides still count.

-

Macadamia Nuts does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only in small amounts when the calories stay under control.

-

D tier.

-

-

-

episode.narrationText:
Nigella Seeds!

-

Ranked!

-

22.3 grams of fat. Saturated fat, omega3, and polyunsaturated fat are doing most of the work. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.

-

44.2 grams of carbs. Starch is doing most of the heavy lifting here. For a seed, this is a very strong sign.

-

16.7 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.

-

Vitamin e at 18% daily value stands out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Magnesium at 92% daily value, iron at 55% daily value, calcium at 30% daily value stand out most. That gives this food real mineral support.

-

On the plus side: usually brings decent fat support. That is one of the category strengths. Often brings dense micronutrient support. That is part of what makes the category interesting. Easy to sprinkle into meals. That practical versatility matters.

-

The drawbacks next: paper scores can overstate realistic serving sizes. People often eat far less than 100 grams. Real serving sizes are often small. Some strong paper numbers are hard to cash out in practice. Texture or prep can be a barrier. Not everyone uses seeds consistently.

-

Nigella Seeds does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best as a support food that boosts meals instead of carrying them alone.

-

B tier.

-

Ranked!

-

-

Outside of that, the profile is pretty quiet.

Pros first: makes meals feel more balanced. The category has real value beyond single-nutrient stats. Helps add volume without much calorie cost. That makes vegetables easier to use often. Good volume for the calories. That matters for satiety and general usefulness.

The drawbacks next: energy density is very low. Good for some use cases, but not enough on its own. Taste and texture can limit compliance. A strong paper profile still needs real-world repeatability. Rarely carries a meal by itself. That is normal here, but still part of the tradeoff.

-

Onion does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only when you need a low-commitment add-on rather than a nutrient-dense anchor.

-

D tier.

episode.narrationText:
Parsnip!

-

Ranked!

-

0.3 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For a tuber, carb behavior is everything.

-

18 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For tubers, the carb side decides whether the food feels stable or flimsy.

-

1.2 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is usually limited here, so the other sections have to carry more.

-

Vitamin c at 19% daily value stands out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Potassium at 11% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

The upsides first: works across a lot of cooking styles. Utility counts for staple carbs. Easy comfort-food base with less baggage than junk food. That practical swap value matters. Can be quite filling. A useful practical strength when the preparation stays sensible.

-

On the weaker side: can go downhill fast when heavily processed. The category has a big preparation trap. Satiety payoff depends a lot on format. Some versions are much steadier than others. Protein support is weak. Tubers still need help from the rest of the meal.

-

Parsnip does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best when you want practical carbs and the rest of the profile is still reasonably clean.

-

B tier.

episode.narrationText:
Pistachios!

-

Ranked!

-

45.3 grams of fat. Saturated fat, omega3, and polyunsaturated fat are doing most of the work. For nuts, fat quality has to justify the calorie density.

-

27.2 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For a nut, fat quality matters a ton.

-

20.2 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein is support here, not the whole argument.

-

Vitamin e at 18% daily value stands out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Magnesium at 30% daily value, zinc at 16% daily value, iron at 22% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still not a major mineral edge.

-

On the plus side: fat and texture help satiety. They can hold up better than many snack foods. Texture helps them feel satisfying. That can make moderation easier than with softer snack foods. Portable, practical snack food. Nuts score real points in life because they are easy to use.

-

Now the downsides: protein is useful but not elite. Nuts help, but they are not protein stars. Portion control can get slippery fast. Dense foods punish casual handful math. Calorie density is very high. That makes portion control a real issue.

-

Pistachios does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only in small amounts when the calories stay under control.

-

C tier.

episode.narrationText:
Plain Yogurt!

-

Ranked!

-

3.3 grams of fat. Cholesterol, saturated fat, and polyunsaturated fat are doing most of the work. For dairy, the fat side can either add richness or drag the whole thing down.

-

4.7 grams of carbs. Sugar and glycemic index matter most here. For dairy, the best versions keep the convenience without wrecking the fat profile.

-

3.5 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Useful protein can rescue a lot of weaker traits here.

-

Vitamin b12 at 18% daily value stands out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Calcium at 12% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

Pros first: easy to fit into familiar meals. That lowers friction for regular use. Easy protein delivery for normal diets. Dairy gets real credit for convenience. Clear calcium identity. That is a core category strength.

-

On the weaker side: tolerance varies a lot person to person. A category strength is less useful if the food does not agree with you. Processing changes the category a lot. The label alone does not tell the whole story. Not everyone tolerates dairy well. That is a real use-case limitation.

-

Plain Yogurt has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when the protein payoff or fermentation angle outweighs the fat and sodium tradeoffs.

-

A tier.

episode.narrationText:
Pumpkin Seeds!

-

Ranked!

-

49 grams of fat. Saturated fat is a major pressure point. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.

-

10.7 grams of carbs. Starch is doing most of the heavy lifting here. For a seed, you want real nutrient concentration, not just tiny-food hype.

-

30.2 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.

-

Vitamin e at 15% daily value stands out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Magnesium at 141% daily value, zinc at 71% daily value, iron at 49% daily value stand out most. That is major mineral support.

-

On the plus side: often brings dense micronutrient support. That is part of what makes the category interesting. Usually brings decent fat support. That is one of the category strengths. Easy to sprinkle into meals. That practical versatility matters.

-

Now the downsides: calories concentrate quickly. Even useful support foods can get dense fast. Calorie density still stacks up fast. Tiny foods can still overshoot fast. Texture or prep can be a barrier. Not everyone uses seeds consistently.

-

Pumpkin Seeds does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best as a support food that boosts meals instead of carrying them alone.

-

B tier.

episode.narrationText:
Ricotta!

-

Ranked!

-

12 grams of fat. Saturated fat is a major pressure point. For dairy, the fat side can either add richness or drag the whole thing down.

-

3 grams of carbs. Sugar and glycemic index matter most here. For a dairy food, that is a strong sign.

-

11.3 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Useful protein can rescue a lot of weaker traits here.

-

Vitamin b12 at 13% daily value, vitamin a at 10% daily value stand out most. That is barely moving the needle.

-

Calcium at 21% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still not a major mineral edge.

-

The upsides first: easy to fit into familiar meals. That lowers friction for regular use. Clear calcium identity. That is a core category strength. Can be a very convenient protein vehicle. Convenience is one of dairy’s strongest practical advantages.

-

On the weaker side: not everyone tolerates dairy well. That is a real use-case limitation. Processing changes the category a lot. The label alone does not tell the whole story. Fat quality varies wildly across dairy. Some dairy is clean, some really is not.

-

Ricotta does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best when the protein payoff or fermentation angle outweighs the fat and sodium tradeoffs.

-

B tier.

episode.narrationText:
Rye!

-

Ranked!

-

1.6 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. Fat is basically not the story here.

-

75.9 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For grains, the carb quality matters much more than the raw number.

-

10.3 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein helps, but not enough if the carb side is weak.

-

The rest of the section is nothing special.

-

Magnesium at 31% daily value, iron at 15% daily value, zinc at 18% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still not a major mineral edge.

-

The upsides first: can keep meals cheap and steady. That is a genuine category strength. Usually affordable and scalable. Practicality matters for staple foods. Easy to batch cook at scale. That practicality is part of why grains matter.

-

On the weaker side: protein quality is limited. Even the better grains usually need pairing. Quality can drop fast with processing. The grain category punishes refinement pretty hard. Needs strong pairings to feel complete. The grain rarely finishes the nutrition job alone.

-

Rye has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want a staple carb that actually brings something useful with it.

-

A tier.

episode.narrationText:
Sesame Seeds!

-

Ranked!

-

49.7 grams of fat. Saturated fat is a major pressure point. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.

-

23.4 grams of carbs. Starch is doing most of the heavy lifting here. For a seed, this is a very strong sign.

-

17.7 grams of protein. Essential amino acid support is one of the better parts here. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.

-

Everything else here is pretty flat.

-

Magnesium at 88% daily value, calcium at 98% daily value, iron at 81% daily value stand out most. That is major mineral support.

-

The upsides first: elite mineral density. The mineral payload is a major category strength beyond a normal seed baseline. Easy to use across lots of foods. Works well in savoury dishes, baking, and toppings. Strong wholefood seed identity. Feels like a very legitimate seed-category food rather than an edge case.

-

Now the downsides: contains some anti-nutrients. Phytates may reduce mineral uptake somewhat. Not suitable for everyone. Sesame allergy risk matters in practice. Saturated fat is not negligible. Still not a disaster, but it is less clean than the best fat-profile seeds.

-

Sesame Seeds does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best as a support food that boosts meals instead of carrying them alone.

-

B tier.

episode.narrationText:
Unsweetened Soy Milk!

-

Ranked!

-

1.8 grams of fat. Polyunsaturated fat is one of the better parts of the profile. For a legume, this is exactly the kind of profile you want.

-

4 grams of carbs. Fibre is where things start to fall off. For legumes, the carbs look much better when fibre and protein are both backing them up.

-

3.3 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein support is a big part of what makes legumes worth it.

-

Everything else here is pretty flat.

-

Minerals are basically not part of the case here.

-

On the plus side: cheap staple with real payoff. This matters because a food is stronger when people can actually use it often. Does a lot of jobs at once. Protein, fibre, and meal utility are why legumes stay valuable. Filling for the calories. Legumes usually earn a lot of practical value from satiety.

-

Now the downsides: dilution makes it less impressive than whole legumes. The legume identity is still there, but not in full strength. Protein quality still has a ceiling. Good, but not meat or dairy level. Texture is not universally loved. That can reduce how often people actually use them.

-

Unsweetened Soy Milk does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best when you want fibre, protein, and actual meal utility together.

-

B tier.

Spinach!

Ranked!

-

2.9 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is not the main pitch here, but extra support still matters.

-

Vitamin k at 402% daily value, vitamin a at 56% daily value, vitamin c at 31% daily value stand out most. That is major vitamin support.

-

Potassium at 12% daily value, magnesium at 19% daily value, iron at 15% daily value stand out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

On the plus side: elite micronutrient density. This is exactly the kind of nutrient-packed vegetable the category is supposed to reward. Very light for the volume. A practical plus for a maintenance-and-repair food. Easy to use in lots of meals. Works raw, cooked, blended, and as a side or add-in.

-

Now the downsides: contains anti-nutrients. Oxalates can reduce mineral usefulness in some contexts. Volume shrinks a lot when cooked. Can make portions feel smaller than expected. Not useful as a fuel food. That is fine for vegetables, but it does limit some use cases.

-

Spinach has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want low downside and easy micronutrient support.

-

episode.narrationText:
Sweet Potato!

-

Ranked!

-

0.1 grams of fat. Omega 3 is doing a lot of the work here. For a tuber, the cleanest win is a more stable carb profile.

-

20.1 grams of carbs. Fibre is doing a lot of the work here. For tubers, the carb side decides whether the food feels stable or flimsy.

-

1.6 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is usually limited here, so the other sections have to carry more.

-

Vitamin a at 160% daily value stands out most. That is major vitamin support.

-

Potassium at 10% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

On the plus side: carotenoid content gives it extra value. That adds a useful plant-pigment angle beyond the basic carb role most tubers play. Fairly filling for the calories. A practical strength for an energy food. Easy to use as a wholefood staple. Works cleanly in meals without needing much rescue from toppings or processing.

-

The drawbacks next: naturally sweeter than some tubers. Still fine, but it is not the lowest-sugar energy food in the category. Healthiness depends on preparation. Heavy added fats or sugary toppings can change the practical outcome. Protein contribution is light. Like most tubers, it is not doing much in the protein lane.

-

Sweet Potato has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want practical carbs and the rest of the profile is still reasonably clean.

-

S tier.

-

-

-

Watermelon Seeds (Unsalted)!

-

Ranked!

-

47.4 grams of fat. Saturated fat is a major pressure point. For seeds, the fat profile is one of the biggest reasons they earn their place.

-

-

28.3 grams of protein. Bioavailability and amino acid quality are both strong. Protein is a bonus, but not enough by itself.

-

The rest of the section is nothing special.

-

Magnesium at 129% daily value, zinc at 71% daily value, iron at 42% daily value stand out most. That is major mineral support.

-

Pros first: easy to sprinkle into meals for a real upgrade. Seeds often shine as support foods. Tiny food with serious nutrient density. Seeds often overperform for their size. Often brings dense micronutrient support. That is part of what makes the category interesting.

-

Now the downsides: texture or prep can be a barrier. Not everyone uses seeds consistently. Real serving sizes are often small. Some strong paper numbers are hard to cash out in practice. Calorie density still stacks up fast. Tiny foods can still overshoot fast.

-

Watermelon Seeds (Unsalted) does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best as a support food that boosts meals instead of carrying them alone.

-

B tier.

episode.narrationText:
White Potato!

-

Ranked!

-

0.1 grams of fat. Saturated fat and omega3 matter most here. For a tuber, this mostly lives or dies on carb behaviour.

-

17.5 grams of carbs. Glycemic index, fibre, and sugar are doing most of the work. For tubers, the carb side decides whether the food feels stable or flimsy.

-

2 grams of protein. Bioavailability is one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is usually limited here, so the other sections have to carry more.

-

Vitamin c at 22% daily value stands out most. That is only mild support overall.

-

Minerals are basically not part of the case here.

-

The upsides first: very practical staple food. Cheap, common, and easy to build meals around, which matters for a tuber category built on energy foods. Can be fairly filling. Especially when eaten in less processed forms. Brings some useful potassium. Not amazing, but enough to matter a bit in the category.

-

Now the downsides: glycemic behaviour is only middling. Not as clean as the best tubers on the carb-behaviour axis. Fibre is only modest. Decent, but not category-leading. Micronutrient return is fine rather than elite. Strong enough to be respectable, not enough to be exceptional.

-

White Potato does have some solid upside. But the tradeoffs keep it from climbing higher. Best when you want practical carbs and the rest of the profile is still reasonably clean.

-

B tier.

-

Whole Wheat has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want a staple carb that actually brings something useful with it.

-

A tier.

-

Yam has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want practical carbs and the rest of the profile is still reasonably clean.

-
